Problem Chosen A 2026 HiMCM Summary Sheet Team Control Number 18213 Choosing a City for High-School Life with Incomplete Evidence Summary We compare sixteen cities for high-school life across ten indicators. Fixed-anchor TOPSIS and maximum regret recommend Oslo under baseline weights and Zurich under equal weights; all sixteen remain possible champions within the retained evidence intervals. An alternative registry counting deﬁnition selects Oslo under both. Ofﬁcial records supplement 25 originally missing city–indicator entries without replacing team values. The mean score-interval width falls from 18.81077 to 15.82233, a 15.89% reduction. The interval revision retains 48 uncertain entries and changes 14 ﬁxed-weight ranks from midpoint completion; separate interior completions let each city lead. Withholding Zurich’s homicide point retains Oslo under baseline weights and selects Oslo under equal weights. Withdrawing its work-commute proxy selects Oslo under both; withdrawing Oslo’s commute proxy alone selects Zurich under both. Withdrawing all twelve means selects Singapore and Zurich, respectively. Both preference proﬁles select Oslo. In 10,000 baseline weight perturbations at Dirichlet concentration 100, Zurich is recommended in 25.48% of draws, compared with 57.38% for Oslo and 17.10% for Singapore. These frequencies are conditional on the chosen weight distribution. Under uniform ten-per-cent development changes, Oslo is selected in all three scenarios under baseline weights; equal weights select Oslo, Zurich and Oslo. City-speciﬁc shocks are illustrative, not forecasts. Country, district and age-group cases distinguish facility supply from student access and broad observed groups from unsupported age-speciﬁc preferences. Keywords: high-school opportunities; TOPSIS; interval evidence; maximum regret; pref- erence sensitivity. . . . . . . . . 26 Team # 18213 1 Page 3 of 27 Introduction and decision scope 1.1 What makes a city suitable for high-school life? A useful comparison connects a student’s school day with the opportunities and con- straints around it. Safety and air quality affect the daily setting; teaching resources and nearby higher education describe educational supply; housing, living costs, transport, travel, broadband and swimming facilities describe household pressures and everyday resources. Our operational deﬁnition of “best” is the conservative choice under these ten criteria, declared weights and retained evidence ranges. It provides a starting recommen- dation for the compared cities, rather than a claim about every student’s experience. The study uses the sixteen cities in the frozen team matrix: Amsterdam, Berlin, Dublin, Helsinki, London, Madrid, Milan, Oslo, Paris, Prague, Singapore, Stockholm, Tokyo, Vienna, Warsaw and Zurich. This is an inherited comparison set across sixteen countries, not a representative sample of all world cities. It exceeds the problem’s minimum of ten cities and spans different resource and cost settings. The ﬁndings concern this set; a broader claim would require an explicit sampling design and additional comparable observations. 1.2 Criterion selection and contribution The ten indicators preserve the agreed team framework and balance education with the conditions that make resources usable in daily life. Their directions and anchors appear in Table 1. Counts and city averages serve as scoped supply or setting measures. They do not directly measure friendships, student wellbeing, school quality, language ﬁt, dis- crimination, cultural participation or individual access. Those outcomes are relevant to a family’s choice; comparable student-level observations are needed to integrate them without inventing measurements or double-counting existing proxies. Our central contribution is a city decision that retains incomplete evidence. We improve source precision, compare a point-completion benchmark with an interval revision, and examine preferences and future conditions without changing the primary indicator set. TOPSIS provides one main quality score; AHP structures stated priorities, Monte Carlo measures speciﬁed perturbations, and VIKOR supplies a focused method comparison. The extensions test the recommendation rather than vote among an expanding set of ranking models. AI assistance supported research retrieval, calculations, code and prose preparation, in- cluding Exa source retrieval and extraction [19, 20]. The appended use report records the known assistance and the outstanding documentation required before submission. 2 Assumptions and their role 1. Comparability follows the retained scope. Original values and population denom- inators remain ﬁxed. Each supplement keeps its provider, year, city boundary and educational population. Mixed-year densities are conditional comparisons; they do not create a same-year census. Team # 18213 Page 4 of 27 2. Utilities are monotone on ﬁxed scales. More resources and less cost or burden improve their respective utilities. Declared anchors set the scale; they are neither estimated preferences nor empirical optimum values. 3. The score permits compensation. Weighted distances combine criteria in a com- mon utility space. The model therefore allows stronger results on some criteria to offset weaker results on others. A family requiring a hard safety or eligibility threshold should apply it separately before choosing. 4. The evidence set is rectangular. Uncertain utilities vary independently within retained intervals. This conservative closure omits unknown cross-criterion and cross-city restrictions. Its possible champions and regret bounds are conditional on this set; they are not population probabilities. 5. Extensions hold the comparison basis ﬁxed. Scenario changes retain population denominators, anchors and the indicated weight rule. They are conditional exper- iments with no ﬁtted future date or representative age-speciﬁc preference distribu- tion. 3 Notation Symbol Meaning M, N w j , a j u ij ℓ ij , h ij L i , U i R i , C κ r Sixteen cities and ten indicators Normalized criterion weight and ﬁxed utility anchor Utility of indicator j for city i, on [0, 1] Retained lower and upper utility bounds Lower and upper TOPSIS score, on [0, 100] Maximum regret and set of possible champions Concentration of a declared Dirichlet weight distribution Raw-value multiplier in a development scenario 4 Data collection and comparability 4.1 A traceable city–indicator matrix We compare M = 16 cities on N = 10 indicators covering safety, environment, household costs, education and everyday resources. Facility supply, commute proxies and school resources remain distinct from adolescent access, school travel and learning quality. 5 Establishing the baseline evaluation model 5.1 Determining indicator weights We retain eight main indicators at weight 0.1125 each and two auxiliary facility indicators, ∑ transport stops and pools, at 0.05 each, so j w j = 1. These weights express a transparent modelling choice. They are not estimated from a student survey. Equal weights provide a separate reference. TOPSIS is the primary score; VIKOR provides a focused method comparison. AHP represents explicit preference scenarios [2], and Monte Carlo measures sensitivity to declared distributions. These extensions retain the same criteria rather than introduce unrelated ranking models. For preference multipliers m j > 0, we use m j w j , w j ′ = ∑ k w k m k A jk = w j ′ . w k ′ (1) The principal eigenvector of A recovers w ′ . With λ max its largest eigenvalue, CI = (λ max − N )/(N − 1) and CR = CI/RI N . Because this matrix is built from exact ratios, λ max = N and CR = 0 up to numerical precision. This veriﬁes internal consistency; it does not establish that these are students’ actual preferences. These conditional data bounds are not sampling conﬁdence intervals, and a conservative recommendation does not identify a uniquely best city. 5.3 Scoring results and interpretation Oslo minimizes maximum regret, followed by Zurich and Singapore (Table 2). Oslo’s lower score bound is 56.43 and its maximum regret is 15.75; Zurich’s corresponding values are 53.97 and 16.94. All sixteen cities remain possible champions, and none is nec- essary. These rankings express a conservative recommendation under the stated criteria and intervals. Holding weights and formulas ﬁxed, evidence for twenty-ﬁve distinct city–indicator cells narrows the average ﬁxed-weight score interval from 18.81077 to 15.82233, a 15.89% reduction. The Oslo bus-stop subset narrows the preceding ﬁxed-weight mean from 15.95582 to 15.82233; the subset is a 2026 inventory with the supplied population. The revised Oslo transport subset changes the baseline conservative recommendation. Withdrawing Singapore’s historical school-stage travel proxy retains Oslo under baseline weights. Evidence improves precision and changes decisions before it necessarily reduces the possible-champion set. As a method diagnostic, TOPSIS and VIKOR use the same illustrative midpoint utilities and weights. VIKOR balances total and largest weighted shortfalls equally and uses sample best/worst values [4]. TOPSIS selects Zurich at the midpoint, whereas VIKOR selects Dublin under ﬁxed weights; Kendall’s τ b = 0.500. Team # 18213 Page 12 of 27 5.4 A signiﬁcant revision: retaining uncertain evidence A controlled comparison shows why evidence bounds belong in the decision. On the same 160 utility entries, compare the midpoint completion z ij = (ℓ ij + h ij )/2 with the retained-interval formulation in Equation 4. Both use identical weights, anchors and TOPSIS scores. The midpoint is a declared diagnostic scenario, rather than an estimate of missing observations or a reconstruction of the team’s historical ﬁrst model. The revision retains 48 non-point entries and selects the city with the smallest worst-case shortfall. Oslo is the ﬁxed-weight recommendation, and 14 cities change decision rank under ﬁxed weights; Kendall’s τ b = 0.617. With equal weights, 14 ranks change and τ b = 0.683. For each target city c, construct a separate interior completion: set every uncertain utility to ℓ ij + α i (h ij − ℓ ij ), with α c = 0.95 and α i = 0.05 for i ̸ = c. All 112 point values remain ﬁxed and all 48 uncertain values lie strictly inside their intervals. Each target ranks ﬁrst under both baseline and equal weights. Across the sixteen targets, the smallest lead is 2.941 score points under baseline weights and 2.222 under equal weights. These separate completions establish feasibility in the declared utility rectangle; they carry no estimated probabilities and do not establish joint physical attainability. Retaining intervals changes the decision order while preserving sixteen possible champi- ons. The 15.89% reduction in interval width comes from admitted data, separately from this formulation comparison. 5.5 Sensitivity to the accepted input information Point withdrawals replace selected point utilities by [0, 1], keeping weights, supplements and the 48 non-point bounds ﬁxed. These conditional ranges are not measured errors or future probabilities. 6 Model revision and extension 6.1 Considering future changes We examine three conditional changes while holding anchors and population denomi- nators ﬁxed. Resource expansion raises higher-education, stop and pool densities by 10%. Living pressure raises living costs, housing cost ratios and travel durations by 10%. Balanced improvement reduces pupil–teacher ratios, PM 2.5 and travel durations by 10%. A comparable multi-year panel is not available, so these changes have no estimated annual rate or forecast date. Team # 18213 Page 19 of 27 A city choice built around a student’s day Our comparison of sixteen cities across ten aspects of high-school life gives families a starting point for weighing everyday trade-offs. Oslo is the cautious recommendation under baseline and education-priority weights; Zurich is selected when all ten measures receive equal weight. The priorities are analyst-designed, not drawn from a student survey. All sixteen cities remain possible leaders, so a family’s choice can depend on the evidence and priorities it considers relevant. How the comparison works The measures cover safety, air quality, housing and living costs, teaching resources, higher education, transport stops, journey time, broadband and swimming facilities. Their units differ: a travel time and a pool count cannot be compared directly. The model puts each measure on a common reference scale, then combines them using the stated priorities. Missing or partial ﬁgures remain ranges instead of being ﬁlled with invented averages. A single completed table could make one city look certain to win even when the missing information matters. We therefore compare each city’s largest possible shortfall behind another city within the retained ranges. The cautious choice is the city with the smallest such shortfall. This gives families a way to discuss trade-offs while keeping uncertain information visible. What new records change Additional evidence narrows the average city-score range by about sixteen per cent while retaining the team’s original values and scoring rules. For Oslo, a 2026 registry provides a source-deﬁned subset of 626 on-street bus stop groups. It replaces the earlier subset of 89 metro stations, rather than being added to it; the comparison uses the supplied 2025 population. Restoring the earlier subset selects Zurich under both baseline and equal weights. This change shows how a source deﬁnition can affect a recommendation, and invites a closer look at what each city count includes. The counts describe supply, not an individual student’s access. A nearby stop may still require a suitable route, service time, fare and accessible connection. A pool count does not describe fees, opening hours or neighbourhood reach. Families can check these details alongside school options, budgets and daily routines. Trying different priorities Setting aside Oslo’s work-commute proxy selects Zurich under both weight sets. In hy- pothetical ten-per-cent changes, baseline weights select Oslo in all three scenarios. Equal weights select Oslo for resource expansion and balanced improvement, and Zurich under living pressure. These are conditional tests of the model, not forecasts or a city’s real chance of being best. The comparison is most useful as a prompt to identify which priorities and local facts matter for a particular student.
